title: Beatrix and the Inheritance
premise: When the coffin of Harborline's founder, Augustus Vane, is exhumed for a centennial ceremony and found empty, night-shift taxi dispatcher Quentin Zhou recognizes the address on the exhumation order as one he dispatched a cab to the night Vane died a hundred years' worth of rumors ago—except it was last month. As Quentin digs into his own dispatch logs, he realizes someone has been using his taxi company to move evidence, witnesses, and possibly a body, exploiting routes only an insider could know. The killer is a fellow dispatcher, Marisol Reyes, who discovered she is Vane's unacknowledged descendant and staged the empty coffin to expose the family that erased her line while covering her own role in a death that followed. In the end, Quentin traps Marisol by feeding her a false route through his dispatch system; she surrenders at the tideline where Vane's true remains surface, and Quentin must choose between turning her in and the truth that survival sometimes costs everything.
about_author: Wren Pemberton spent a decade answering phones for a coastal transit company before trading the headset for a writing desk, and still keeps a tide chart pinned above it. Their novels are known for ordinary workers who stumble into extraordinary crimes and can't help solving them.

chapters.title: The Empty Box
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Quentin's POV. On his night shift, Quentin hears radio chatter about the exhumation of town founder Augustus Vane: the coffin is empty. A cab he dispatched was parked near the cemetery that night. The beat is unease—the moment routine cracks open into something wrong.

chapters.title: Dispatch Log 4471
chapters.summary: Quentin pulls his own logs and finds a fare to the Vane mausoleum at 2:14 a.m., logged under a name that doesn't exist. His supervisor tells him to drop it. Emotional beat: professional pride curdling into obsession—he never takes a case he can't close.

chapters.title: The Founder's Shadow
chapters.summary: Quentin visits the Vane historical society and meets archivist Edith Vane-Cole, the founder's great-granddaughter, who is furious about the exhumation but oddly unsurprised. POV shifts briefly to Edith. The beat: first hint that the Vane family hides something older than murder.

chapters.title: Fare Unknown
chapters.summary: Quentin tracks the driver of the 2:14 a.m. fare, Tommy Okafor, who remembers a woman in a gray coat who paid cash and asked him to wait with the engine running. Beat: dread—someone used his company as an instrument, and he let them.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: A hand washes up at Gull Point—not Vane's, forensics say, but recent. Detective Ilsa Brandt interviews Quentin, suspicious of how much he knows about dispatch patterns. Beat: Quentin becomes a suspect in his own investigation.

chapters.title: Night Shift Confessions
chapters.summary: Quentin and fellow dispatcher Marisol Reyes share coffee in the break room; she's warm, sharp, and asks unsettlingly precise questions about the log system. Beat: false comfort—the reader meets the antagonist as a friend.

chapters.title: The Centennial File
chapters.summary: Edith shows Quentin sealed family papers: a second child born out of wedlock, written out of the will in 1919. Beat: the mystery deepens from a stolen body to a stolen identity across generations.

chapters.title: Route Nineteen
chapters.summary: Quentin notices Route 19—a dead-end coastal road—appears in altered logs on three separate nights. Someone with dispatcher access edits history. Beat: paranoia; the killer is inside the building.

chapters.title: Tommy Goes Quiet
chapters.summary: Tommy Okafor misses his shift; his apartment is cleaned out. Quentin finds a taxi receipt tucked in Tommy's mailbox with a phone number scrawled on it. Beat: guilt hardens into resolve—his witness, his responsibility.

chapters.title: Brandt's Bargain
chapters.summary: Detective Brandt offers Quentin informal immunity in exchange for access to dispatch records. He hesitates—handing over the logs means admitting his own negligence. Beat: love of the job against duty to the truth.

chapters.title: The Gray Coat
chapters.summary: Cemetery security footage surfaces: the woman in gray is recognizable only by posture and a distinctive way of holding a pen. Quentin freezes—it's how Marisol signs off her shift reports. Beat: betrayal lands like a physical blow.

chapters.title: Blood and Ledger
chapters.summary: Quentin secretly checks Marisol's employment file and finds forged references—then finds a birth certificate naming her a descendant of Vane's erased daughter. Beat: motive revealed; sympathy tangles with horror.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Quentin confronts Marisol on the break-room roof. She admits nothing but tells him a story about families that survive by burying their own. Beat: the antagonist becomes fully human; Quentin wavers.

chapters.title: The Second Grave
chapters.summary: Following Route 19, Quentin finds a shallow grave containing Tommy Okafor—and beside it, a century-old skeleton wearing a founder's ring. Vane was never in the coffin either. Beat: the case doubles; grief and awe.

chapters.title: Edith's Silence
chapters.summary: Edith confesses the family knew the coffin was empty for decades and maintained the lie to protect the estate. She begs Quentin to stop. Beat: duty versus compassion—everyone surviving has blood on their hands.

chapters.title: Trap on the Wire
chapters.summary: Quentin broadcasts a fake dispatch: a 'witness' being driven to safekeeping via Route 19 at dawn. Only someone monitoring the system would intercept. Beat: hunter becomes bait; tension coils tight.

chapters.title: Interception
chapters.summary: Marisol takes the bait, but so does a panicked Edith's lawyer, and the two nearly collide at the cliff turnoff. Marisol holds Quentin at knifepoint in his own cab. Beat: climax ignites—killer and investigator face to face in the space between them.

chapters.title: What the Sea Took Back
chapters.summary: Marisol forces Quentin to drive to the tideline where she buried what remained of Vane; the morning tide is already uncovering it. She explains: exposure of the family meant exposing herself first. Beat: confession as tragedy—survival demanded the crime.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: With sirens approaching, Quentin must decide: arrest her or let the sea take the story. He chooses duty—but promises to tell the whole truth, including the Vanes'. Beat: theme crystallized; love against duty resolved through honesty rather than mercy alone.

chapters.title: Booking
chapters.summary: Marisol surrenders without a fight; Brandt arrests Edith and the lawyer too. Quentin gives his full statement, implicating himself in the cover-up of his logging failures. Beat: cost paid—the price of survival is accountability.

chapters.title: Reburial
chapters.summary: Vane's remains are laid to rest publicly, with Marisol's lineage read aloud in court filings. Quentin attends in civilian clothes, unrecognized. Beat: quiet catharsis—identity restored, however late.

chapters.title: Last Call
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Quentin works another quiet night shift, the headset humming. A caller asks for a ride to the cemetery. He sends a cab, then writes the first page of the true account. Beat: resolution—the case closed, the storyteller changed.
